newsitem.title: USA: LatAm markets seen volatile short term - analysts.
newsitem.headline: LatAm markets seen volatile short term - analysts.

text.p: Slumping Latin American markets are likely to be choppy in coming weeks amid worries about Brazil's currency, analysts said Friday.

They added that markets shaken by Brazil in a so-called "samba effect" remained fundamentally sound. However, they were being undermined by jitters among foreign investors about emerging market currencies around the world.
"It's going to take a few days for people to regain their confidence in (Brazil's) currency," said Geoffrey Dennis, global emerging markets strategist at HSBC James Capel.
"There is going to be a lot of volatility ... and a lot of that volatility is going to be downward," he said in an interview from London.
Francois Gour, Latin American equity strategist at Caspian Securities, said the skid was a "typical short-term panic" unrelated to Latin America's fundamental strengths.
"Our hope is that over the next few weeks people will ... start to realize that the threat of a (Brazilian) devaluation is not so high," he said.
Led by Brazil, Latin American markets dropped in recent days after having been among the best-performing in the world this year.

According to the Morgan Stanley Capital International Index, Latin American markets overall were off 7.2 percent from their 52-week highs as of the close of business Thursday. The index had risen 48.5 percent this year through its peak July 10.
Sao Paulo's Bovespa exchange, an investors' darling as its 47-stock index rose 86 percent this year, was off 12.7 percent from its high.
The Bovespa fell still further Friday, tumbling almost four percent by early afternoon. Both Mexico's IPC share index and Argentina's Merval index dropped more than 1.8 percent.
Concerns about Brazil's currency and profit-taking after a steady runup were the key reason for Sao Paulo's drop and the shock waves through the region, analysts and fund managers said.

Investors scarred by the 1994 Mexican peso devaluation are worried that the weakness recently shown by such emerging market currencies as the Thai baht and Polish zloty could spread to the Brazil real.

When Latin American fund managers "see a problem in one country they think it's going to spill over to another country," said Eric Anderson, a senior portfolio manager at ING Investment Management in Atlanta.

Latin American stocks remain fundamentally attractive despite the volatility, largely because of their cheap prices, analysts and managers said. In addition, Latin American countries have carried out reforms, such as slashing inflation and opening their economies to competition, that make them better draws for investment than even a few years ago.

"In the short term, I think there has been a lot of (speculative short-term) hot or hedge fund money in Brazil that got nervous and got out," said Antonio Docal, co-portfolio manager of the Evergreen Latin American Fund in Boston.
"For six months (ahead) and longer, I'm pretty confident."

The analysts said the domino effect of one Latin American market or economy -- in the current case, Brazil -- rattling others in the region would continue until the countries had higher levels of savings.
Higher savings would mean the markets would not be so dependent on foreign capital for funding, they said.
